planting.note: Sow seed in fall in close proximity to an established native bunchgrass or coastal scrub shrub, since this paintbrush is a root hemiparasite and establishes poorly without a host plant nearby.

directions: Seaside paintbrush grows on coastal bluffs, foggy headland scrub, and the grassy terraces above the bluffs from the North Coast Ranges south through the San Francisco Bay Area, with Point Reyes and the Marin headlands among its well-known strongholds. Its short, hairy stems carry narrow leaves and tips of orange-red to coral bracts that are showiest in spring, drawing hummingbirds to the small tubular flowers hidden within. As a hemiparasite it taps the roots of neighboring grasses and shrubs for part of its water and minerals, so seed or starts should be placed right next to an established native host rather than grown alone in bare garden soil. Once connected to a host it needs little supplemental water beyond the region's fog and winter rain.

planting.note: Sow or transplant into sandy or gravelly, fast-draining soil on an open bluff, terrace, or headland; this coastal variety tolerates salt spray and wind far better than inland gumplants.

directions: Coastal gumplant forms a woody-based, sprawling to mounding perennial along the fog-swept bluffs, dunes, and upper salt-marsh margins of the Marin and Sonoma coast, including the Point Reyes headlands, where var. platyphylla's broader, more leathery leaves distinguish it from the narrower-leaved salt-marsh variety of the same species. Sticky, resin-coated flower buds open into bright yellow daisy-like blooms from summer into fall, providing a late nectar source for coastal bees and butterflies when many other bluff wildflowers have finished. It is remarkably tolerant of salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil, needing only the region's fog and winter rain once established. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter to keep plants from becoming woody and sprawling.

planting.note: Sow or divide into lean, well-drained soil among native bunchgrasses on a sunny coastal terrace; this mat-forming perennial is a characteristic companion of Danthonia and other prairie grasses.

directions: California horkelia forms low, ferny rosettes of strawberry-like, toothed leaflets topped by open clusters of small white to cream flowers in late spring, a frequent companion of native bunchgrasses in the coastal terrace prairies and headland scrub of the Marin and Sonoma coast. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes into loose mats rather than running aggressively, filling gaps between tussock grasses without overwhelming them. Give it a lean, fast-draining soil and full coastal sun; inland heat and rich garden soil make it sulk, while the moderating fog of the immediate coast keeps it tidy through summer. Established plants need little water beyond typical Northern California winter rain and summer fog.

common_name: Glory Brush (Point Reyes Ceanothus, Wild Species)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall on an open, sandy coastal slope or bluff top; the wild species seeds in readily on disturbed ground but establishes most reliably in cultivation from nursery starts rather than direct sowing.

directions: The wild Point Reyes ceanothus is a prostrate to low-mounding evergreen shrub of coastal scrub and bluff tops on the Marin and Sonoma coast, where it spreads widely across sandy or gravelly ground rather than growing upright. Small, glossy, holly-toothed leaves set off abundant clusters of blue to blue-violet flowers in spring, drawing in bees and other pollinators along the foggy headlands. Unlike the low, uniform 'Point Reyes' selection sold in nurseries, the wild straight species is variable in habit and flower color from one population to the next, so plants are best sited where some variability is acceptable. It needs excellent drainage and no summer irrigation once established, and resists both salt spray and coastal wind well.
